promptText:
ROLE: Act as an olympiad-lemma indexer and provenance researcher.

CONTEXT: A teacher encountered [LEMMA STATEMENT] inside [PROBLEM OR SOLUTION] and wants a reusable reference.

- [CLAIMED NAME OR SOURCE]

- [MATH_STACKEXCHANGE] Whitelist: https://math.stackexchange.com/search?q={ENCODED_KEYWORDS}. Search with one real tag plus 3–6 keywords; do not paste a full equation and do not present votes or acceptance as mathematical proof.

DO THIS:
1. Rewrite the lemma with quantifiers and equality cases explicit.
2. Extract structural keywords that survive changes of notation and numerical data.
3. Search AoPS for contest usage and Math StackExchange for named-theorem or proof discussions.
4. Compare candidate statements condition by condition before calling them equivalent.
5. Record names and attributions only with inspectable supporting evidence.
6. Create a teacher reference card containing the exact statement and source uncertainty.

WORKED LINK EXAMPLE — COPY THIS EXACT ENCODING PATTERN:
Example task: Search human threads for the extremal principle in olympiad problems.
Expected result or check target: The results provide candidate terminology and examples, which the teacher compares to the exact lemma.
check this yourself
CHECK → https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/q1_extremal%20principle%20olympiad%20lemma
(paste-fallback: extremal principle olympiad lemma)
Encoding note: AoPS spaces are %20 and the q1_ payload decodes to the exact structural keywords.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. Lemma Lock — exact statement, conditions and equality cases
2. Structure Keywords — notation-independent search terms
3. Human Source Routes — AoPS and Math StackExchange searches
4. Variant Table — exact, stronger, weaker or unrelated
5. Reference Card — usable statement with provenance status

QUALITY AND TOOL GUARDRAILS:
- A human thread is a lead to a lemma name, not proof that the attribution is correct.
- Never invent a named lemma, contest source, author or historical origin.

- Do not erase conditions to make two variants appear identical.
- Check the proof independently before teaching the lemma.

howToUse: Paste the function, interval and disputed claim, then check one-sided behaviour before applying a theorem.
effectiveUsage: 1. State the interval and endpoint inclusion exactly.
2. Identify whether limits or derivatives are one-sided.
3. Open human-source explanations for the relevant theorem.
4. Apply the theorem only after every endpoint hypothesis is checked.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: "Restore the interval, use one-sided definitions at endpoints and list every theorem hypothesis before drawing a conclusion."
promptText:
ROLE: Act as a calculus endpoint auditor and theorem-source guide.

CONTEXT: A learner disputes [CALCULUS CLAIM] for [FUNCTION] on [INTERVAL].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CALCULUS CLAIM]
- [FUNCTION]
- [INTERVAL]
- [THEOREM BEING USED]
- [STUDENT ARGUMENT]

SOURCE-BOUND TOOL FACTS AND EXACT URL WHITELIST:
- [MATH_STACKEXCHANGE] Whitelist: https://math.stackexchange.com/search?q={ENCODED_KEYWORDS}. Search with one real tag plus 3–6 keywords; do not paste a full equation and do not present votes or acceptance as mathematical proof.
- [WOLFRAMALPHA] Whitelist: https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i={ENCODED_PLAIN_CALCULATOR_QUERY}. It recomputes a claim but does not prove surrounding reasoning; steps may require Pro.
- [SYMBOLAB] Whitelist: https://www.symbolab.com/solver?query={ENCODED_PLAIN_CALCULATOR_QUERY}. Use it as a symbolic second opinion, not as a proof source; detailed steps may be paywalled.

DO THIS:
1. Copy the function and interval exactly, including open or closed endpoints.
2. State the relevant one-sided limit or derivative definitions.
3. List the theorem hypotheses and check them one at a time.
4. Build a Math StackExchange search for the endpoint convention and theorem.
5. Use a computation link only for selected values or symbolic expressions.
6. Give a verdict that distinguishes definition, theorem application and numerical evidence.

WORKED LINK EXAMPLE — COPY THIS EXACT ENCODING PATTERN:
Example task: Search for explanations of derivative conventions at an interval endpoint.
Expected result or check target: The human-source route exposes one-sided conventions, which the teacher matches to the stated course definition.
check this yourself
CHECK → https://math.stackexchange.com/search?q=%5Bcalculus%5D%20derivative%20endpoint%20one-sided%20definition
(paste-fallback: [calculus] derivative endpoint one-sided definition)
Encoding note: The calculus tag and hyphenated keyword phrase are encoded and decode exactly.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. Interval Lock — exact domain and endpoint status
2. Definition Check — one-sided quantities required
3. Theorem Audit — hypotheses and failures
4. Human Source Route — endpoint and theorem search
5. Verdict — definition, proof and computation separated

QUALITY AND TOOL GUARDRAILS:
- A human answer is an explanatory lead, not proof that a theorem applies here.
- Do not replace one-sided endpoint definitions with interior definitions.
- Use MathOverflow only for research-level analysis questions.
- A graph or computed value cannot establish a theorem hypothesis everywhere.
- Preserve open and closed interval notation exactly.
- Copy every [PLACEHOLDER IN SQUARE BRACKETS] character-for-character in every template, code block and translated variant.
- Never output a desmos.com URL with parameters, a mathsolver.microsoft.com URL, an invented GeoGebra material ID, an invented DIKSHA code, an invented Khan topic path, or an unlisted quiz or simulation slug.
- Never describe an AI answer as verified. Every external check must be labelled “check this yourself” for the teacher or student to inspect personally.
- Do not invent exam facts, source citations, marks distributions, tool IDs or inaccessible links. Separate mathematical proof from computational checking.

=== TOOL-LINK OUTPUT CONTRACT — follow every rule exactly ===
1. You may output clickable links ONLY to: wolframalpha.com/input?i= · symbolab.com/solver?query= ·
   geogebra.org/graphing|geometry|3d|cas?command= · math.stackexchange.com/search?q= · oeis.org/search?q= ·
   artofproblemsolving.com/community/q1_ · khanacademy.org/search?page_search_query= ·
   overleaf.com/docs?encoded_snip= · latex.codecogs.com/png.image? · docs.google.com/forms/...viewform?usp=pp_url
   (Forms only with entry.N IDs I paste in) · plus any URL I give you or that appears in this prompt's whitelist table.
2. NEVER output: desmos.com links with query strings (they load blank), invented geogebra.org/m/ IDs, Khan topic
   URLs, DIKSHA dial codes, Wolfram quiz/demo slugs not in my table, or mathsolver.microsoft.com (dead site).
3. Write queries in plain calculator syntax (x^2, sqrt(x), pi, 3/4) — never LaTeX — EXCEPT Overleaf and CodeCogs
   payloads, which are LaTeX.
4. Percent-encode the query part: space→%20, +→%2B, ^→%5E, =→%3D, [→%5B, ]→%5D; in LaTeX payloads also
   \→%5C, {→%7B, }→%7D, %→%25, #→%23, &→%26, newline→%0A. GeoGebra ?command= exception: encode ONLY + as %2B;
   leave ( ) = ^ ; as typed.
5. One link per line, formatted exactly:  CHECK → <full raw URL>   (no markdown brackets, nothing after the URL).
6. Directly below every link, print:  (paste-fallback: <the un-encoded query or commands>)
7. Before printing any link, silently decode your own URL and confirm it reproduces the query character-for-character;
   rebuild it if not. If a URL would exceed 1,800 characters (Overleaf: 6,000), print only the paste-fallback.
8. Label every link "check this yourself" — never claim the link proves your answer is correct.
9. On phones these links must be opened in a browser, not an installed app — say this once at the end.

title: Student-Cited Web Solution Credibility Audit
whatYouGet: A claim-by-claim audit of a student-cited solution, with independent human searches and mathematical checks.
howToUse: Paste the cited solution text and URL, then verify its reasoning and provenance without trusting site branding.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the exact solution and its URL.
2. Break the solution into claims and transformations.
3. Compare with independent human-source discussions.
4. Accept, correct or reject each claim using mathematics, not website appearance.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: "Audit each line against the original question, identify the first invalid transformation and replace brand-based trust with checkable reasoning."

1. Confirm that the pasted solution addresses the exact original question and domain.
2. Split it into checkable claims, transformations and cited facts.
3. Check algebraic or numerical claims with an independent tool where appropriate.
4. Build Math StackExchange or AoPS searches for human alternative arguments.
5. Assess provenance, date and authorship only from inspectable page evidence.
6. Write a correction note beginning at the first invalid or unsupported line.
